sources.title: NGSS MS-ESS2-5: Collect data to provide evidence for how the motions and complex interactions of air masses result in changes in weather conditions
NOAA JetStream: How to read Surface Weather Maps

note.text: This is a slice through the air, seen from the side. An air mass is a huge body of air with the same temperature and humidity.
A front is where two air masses meet. At a cold front, cold air is pushing in and replacing warm air.
note.remember: Cold front: cold air replaces warm.

steps.title: Cold air
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow of cold air moving in from the left.

note.text: Cold air is denser than warm air, so it stays low and wedges under the warm air like a snowplow.

steps.title: Warm air
steps.instruction: Draw the arrow of warm air forced up over the front.

note.text: The steep cold front forces the warm air up quickly. Rising air cools, and its water vapor condenses.
The fast-rising air builds tall clouds along a narrow band: showers and thunderstorms.
On weather maps, a cold front is drawn as a blue line with triangles pointing the way it's moving.

steps.title: Name the parts
steps.instruction: Pick the name for each numbered part.

mistakes.Warm air mass: This air is behind the front, wedging in low: it's the cold air mass.

steps.title: Read the data
steps.question: At 3 pm it's 75 °F with south winds. A line of storms passes. At 9 pm it's 45 °F, skies are clear, and winds blow from the northwest. What happened?

options.text: A cold front passed, and a cold air mass replaced the warm one
options.feedback: Yes. Storms, then falling temperatures, clearing skies and a wind shift are signs of a cold front passing.
A warm front brings warmer air. Here the temperature dropped 30 degrees.

options.text: Nothing changed but the time of day
options.feedback: Evening cools things a little, but a 30-degree drop with a wind shift means a new air mass arrived.
A stationary front wouldn't bring such a quick, big change.

steps.title: Why storms?
steps.question: Why do cold fronts often bring thunderstorms?

options.text: Dense cold air forces warm, moist air up quickly, and it cools to form tall clouds
options.feedback: Right. The steep front lifts the warm air fast, so tall storm clouds build in a narrow band.
The storms come from warm, moist air being forced up, not from the cold air itself.

options.text: Warm air sinks under the cold air
options.feedback: It's the reverse: warm air is less dense and gets pushed up.
The key is air masses colliding: cold air lifting warm air.
